question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release (population trend / vital statistics).
target.publisher: Statistics Korea (KOSTAT), via the monthly Population Trends / Vital Statistics release
target.cadence: monthly, with a lag of roughly 2–3 months after the reference month
target.caveats: The target period is completed relative to the 2026-08-23 cutoff, but the official July 2026 figure is not yet published. The first report may be provisional and subject to revision. The definition is live births occurring in South Korea (domestic), not births to Korean nationals abroad. If the ques

candidates.perspective: Statistics Korea monthly vital statistics time series
candidates.hypothesis: July 2026 births can be projected from the same month in prior years plus recent monthly momentum. July is typically a high-birth month in Korea; the year-over-year change in recent months constrains the level.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live births for South Korea for July 2021, July 2022, July 2023, July 2024, July 2025, and all months from January 2025 through June 2026 (or the latest available months before the cutoff). Minimum evidence: the July values for the last 3–5 years and the most recent 6–12 monthly values.

candidates.perspective: Marriage registrations as a leading indicator of births
candidates.hypothesis: In South Korea, first births are strongly associated with marriage, typically 1–2 years earlier. Marriage registrations in mid-2024 to mid-2025 can help predict July 2026 births, especially if recent marriage trends have shifted.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly marriage registrations in South Korea for 2024 and 2025, and if available 2026 year-to-date. Minimum evidence: monthly marriage counts for at least 2024–2025 to estimate the lagged relationship.

candidates.perspective: Population and women of childbearing age
candidates.hypothesis: Births equal the number of women of childbearing age multiplied by age-specific fertility rates. Changes in the size and age structure of the female population aged 15–49, especially 25–39, constrain the expected number of births.
candidates.data_to_find: South Korean female population by single year of age for 2025 or 2026, and age-specific fertility rates (ASFR) for recent years. Minimum evidence: female population aged 20–39 and total fertility rate or ASFR for 2024–2025.
search_hints: South Korea female population by age 2025

candidates.perspective: Birth registration records and resident registration
candidates.hypothesis: Births are registered with local governments; the number of birth registrations in July 2026 (or around that month) may be available from administrative sources before the official vital statistics release, though registration timing can lag occurrence.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly birth registration counts from the Ministry of the Interior and Safety (행정안전부) resident registration statistics for July 2026, or weekly/monthly provisional birth counts. Minimum evidence: any administrative monthly birth count for July 2026 or June 2026.

candidates.perspective: Policy and calendar effects on births
candidates.hypothesis: Government pronatalist policies, changes in parental leave, or one-off events (e.g., a temporary baby bonus) could shift births in 2026. Also, the timing of the 2026 Lunar New Year and other holidays may affect birth seasonality.
candidates.data_to_find: Announcements of major new birth incentives effective in 2025–2026, and any evidence of their measured impact on monthly births. Minimum evidence: a list of major policy changes and any reported birth response.

candidates.perspective: Official and private forecasts for 2026 births
candidates.hypothesis: Statistics Korea or research institutes may publish monthly or annual birth projections for 2026. These forecasts can anchor the July 2026 estimate, though they may be based on models rather than observed data.
candidates.data_to_find: Any published forecast for South Korea's 2026 total births or monthly births, including from KOSTAT's population projections or private research. Minimum evidence: a 2026 annual birth forecast or a monthly path.

candidates.perspective: Seasonal adjustment factors for monthly births
candidates.hypothesis: The ratio of July births to the annual total or to adjacent months is stable enough to use as a seasonal factor. This allows converting an annual estimate or a year-to-date total into a July figure.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live birth totals for South Korea for several recent years (e.g., 2019–2025) to compute the average July share of annual births and the July-to-June ratio. Minimum evidence: at least 3 years of monthly data.

candidates.perspective: Year-to-date births and recent monthly changes
candidates.hypothesis: If year-to-date births for 2026 (January–June) are available, July can be estimated by applying the historical July-to-June ratio or the recent month-over-month growth rate.
candidates.data_to_find: Cumulative live births for January–June 2026, or monthly births for January–June 2026, from KOSTAT or administrative sources. Minimum evidence: at least the most recent month's births and the year-to-date total.

directions.hypothesis: If the July 2026 birth level is driven by marriages 1–2 years earlier, a quantified lag distribution (share of births occurring 12–24 months after marriage) would convert the strong 2024–2025 marriage surge (p8, p22, p24) into a July 2026 birth increment. This unlocks the d3 route and would resolve whether the 2025 birth recovery continues into mid-2026.

p1.role: July 2025 live births in South Korea (21,803)

a1.role: ratio of July 2026 births to July 2025 births

methods.rationale: Anchors on the observed July 2025 level (p1) and applies a decelerated y/y change factor (a1) grounded in the 2025 monthly momentum (p16–p21) and marriage surge (p8, p22, p24). Shared dependency: p1 is the same KOSTAT measurement underlying p2/p26; the main failure mode is that the 2025 recovery stalls or reverses in 2026, which the wide a1 band partly covers.

p4.role: Jan–Jul 2025 cumulative live births (147,804) used as a scale proxy for the 2026 annual level

methods.rationale: Uses the Jan–Jul 2025 cumulative (p4) as a scale anchor and the assumed July seasonal share (a2) to back out a July level. This is a weaker route because p4 is a 2025 partial-year total, not a 2026 annual total; it serves as a seasonality-based cross-check on m1 rather than a primary estimate. Failure mode: July seasonality or the 2026 level diverges from the 2025 base.

assumptions.name: July 2026 y/y birth change factor vs July 2025
assumptions.rationale: July 2025 births were 21,803 (p1/p2). The 2025 monthly y/y birth changes decelerated from +9.9% (Sep, p19) to +2.1% (Oct, p16) with a +6.1% Jan–Oct cumulative (p18), and the marriage surge (p8, p22, p24) supports continued but moderating growth into 2026. A central +4% with a wide band spanning flat-to-+10% reflects this deceleration and the absence of any 2026 observation.
assumptions.applies_when: The 2025 birth recovery continues into July 2026 at a decelerated pace, with no major policy or shock discontinuity.
assumptions.falsified_by: Any 2026 monthly birth release showing y/y change outside roughly −2% to +10%, or evidence of a sharp reversal in the marriage-led recovery.

assumptions.name: July share of annual births
assumptions.rationale: July is a seasonally high birth month in Korea; the July share of the annual total is needed to convert an annual 2026 estimate into a July figure. No kept point supplies this share directly, so it is assumed with a wide band consistent with typical Korean birth seasonality.
assumptions.applies_when: An annual 2026 birth total is available or estimated and July seasonality is stable.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published monthly distribution showing July's share materially outside 7.8–9.4%.

Critically, the snapshot dates (2025-09-24, 2025-11-26) show these are July 2025 values, not July 2026; the '2026' period labels attached to p1-p15 are a provenance error and must not be read as the target.

July 2025 deaths 27,979 (-0.7%), natural decline 6,175, divorces 7,826 (-1.4%). Internally consistent (27,979 - 21,803 = 6,176, rounding), which confirms the 21,803 birth figure is the same release's number. Not inputs to the birth estimate.

Monthly y/y birth growth rates through 2025: Oct 2025 +2.1% (+426), Sep 2025 +9.9%, Mar 2025 +0.8%, with Oct 2024 +8.2% as the base effect. Together they show a decelerating but still positive 2025 momentum, which is the key transfer signal for 2026.
Jan-Oct 2025 cumulative 205,257, +6.1% y/y — consistent with the +7.2% Jan-Jul figure (p4/p28) and the monthly deceleration in p16/p19.
Marriage surge: Oct 2025 +18.2% (+2,600), April 2025 peak +24.6%. Same underlying KOSTAT marriage series as p8/p9 but different months; supports the d3 lag route.

January 2026 release (snapshot 2026-07-17): births 23,947, +2,486 (+11.6%); marriages +0.7%; TFR 0.88 (+0.08); ASFR 30-34 = 81.1 (+8.0) and 35-39 = 56.6 (+9.3). This is the only genuinely 2026-vintage evidence and shows the recovery continuing strongly into 2026, though the marriage growth has flattened.
2025 annual births 238,343, +3.6% vs 2023 — a different comparison base (2023, not 2024) and a different period (annual), so it is context for the level, not a direct y/y signal.

p1.role: July 2025 live births in South Korea (the observed prior-year level for the same calendar month, used as the base to be carried forward)

a1.role: ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births in South Korea

methods.rationale: Primary route: carry forward the observed July 2025 level (21,803, p1) with a y/y change factor grounded in the 2026 evidence (p35/p36) and the 2025 deceleration (p16, p19, p24, p38). Shared dependency: p1 is the same release vintage as p2-p5, so any revision to the July 2025 base propagates here. Failure mode: if the 2025 recovery stalls in 2026, a1's central value is too high.

p4.role: January-July 2025 cumulative live births in South Korea (the observed prior-year cumulative base)

a3.role: ratio of January-July 2026 cumulative live births to January-July 2025 cumulative live births in South Korea

a2.role: ratio of July 2026 live births to January-July 2026 cumulative live births in South Korea

methods.rationale: Cumulative-to-month route: scale the kept Jan-Jul 2025 cumulative (147,804, p4) by the 2026 cumulative y/y factor and apply the July-to-cumulative seasonal ratio. This uses the cumulative series rather than the single July month, giving a partially independent check on m1. Shared dependency: both routes lean on the same 2026 momentum evidence (p35/p36, p16, p19, p38), so they are correlated. Failure mode: the July-to-cumulative ratio is estimated from a single year (2025) and may drift.

assumptions.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births in South Korea
assumptions.rationale: Anchored on kept evidence: January 2026 births were +11.6% y/y (p35/p36), but the 2025 monthly y/y rate decelerated from +9.9% in September to +2.1% in October (p19, p16) and the marriage y/y rate fell from +24.6% in April 2025 (p24) to +0.7% in January 2026 (p38), so the mid-2026 increment should be smaller than January's. A central +5% with a 10-90 band of roughly -2% to +13% reflects genuine uncertainty about whether the 2025 recovery persists into July 2026.
assumptions.applies_when: July 2026 births are driven by the same marriage-cohort and policy momentum observed through January 2026, with no new shock between February and July 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published 2026 monthly birth figure for February-June 2026 showing y/y growth outside roughly -2% to +13%, or a collapse in 2026 marriage registrations.

assumptions.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to January-July 2026 cumulative live births in South Korea
assumptions.rationale: From kept evidence, July 2025 births (21,803, p1) divided by Jan-Jul 2025 cumulative births (147,804, p4) is about 0.1475. This within-year seasonal ratio converts a 2026 cumulative total into a July figure; the band reflects year-to-year variation in the seasonal profile.
assumptions.applies_when: The 2026 within-year birth profile through July resembles 2025's, so July's share of the cumulative total is stable.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2026 monthly pattern showing a materially different July concentration, e.g. a large one-off shift in spring or summer births.

assumptions.name: Ratio of January-July 2026 cumulative live births to January-July 2025 cumulative live births in South Korea
assumptions.rationale: Anchored on kept evidence: January 2026 births were +11.6% y/y (p35/p36), while the 2025 monthly y/y rate decelerated to +2.1% by October (p16, p19) and the marriage y/y rate fell to +0.7% in January 2026 (p38). A central +7% for the seven-month cumulative, with a 10-90 band of 0% to +14%, reflects the fading 2025 base effects and the uncertain persistence of the marriage-driven recovery.
assumptions.applies_when: The 2026 y/y birth growth through July averages near the January 2026 rate but decays toward the late-2025 pace, with no new shock.
assumptions.falsified_by: Published 2026 monthly birth figures for February-June 2026 implying cumulative y/y growth outside roughly 0% to +14%.

kept.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births in South Korea
kept.rationale: Anchored on kept evidence: January 2026 births were +11.6% y/y (p35/p36), but the 2025 monthly y/y rate decelerated from +9.9% in September to +2.1% in October (p19, p16) and the marriage y/y rate fell from +24.6% in April 2025 (p24) to +0.7% in January 2026 (p38), so the mid-2026 increment should b
kept.applies_when: July 2026 births are driven by the same marriage-cohort and policy momentum observed through January 2026, with no new shock between February and July 2026.
kept.falsified_by: A published 2026 monthly birth figure for February-June 2026 showing y/y growth outside roughly -2% to +13%, or a collapse in 2026 marriage registrations.

kept.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to January-July 2026 cumulative live births in South Korea
kept.rationale: From kept evidence, July 2025 births (21,803, p1) divided by Jan-Jul 2025 cumulative births (147,804, p4) is about 0.1475. This within-year seasonal ratio converts a 2026 cumulative total into a July figure; the band reflects year-to-year variation in the seasonal profile.
kept.applies_when: The 2026 within-year birth profile through July resembles 2025's, so July's share of the cumulative total is stable.
kept.falsified_by: A 2026 monthly pattern showing a materially different July concentration, e.g. a large one-off shift in spring or summer births.

kept.name: Ratio of January-July 2026 cumulative live births to January-July 2025 cumulative live births in South Korea
kept.rationale: Anchored on kept evidence: January 2026 births were +11.6% y/y (p35/p36), while the 2025 monthly y/y rate decelerated to +2.1% by October (p16, p19) and the marriage y/y rate fell to +0.7% in January 2026 (p38). A central +7% for the seven-month cumulative, with a 10-90 band of 0% to +14%, reflects
kept.applies_when: The 2026 y/y birth growth through July averages near the January 2026 rate but decays toward the late-2025 pace, with no new shock.
kept.falsified_by: Published 2026 monthly birth figures for February-June 2026 implying cumulative y/y growth outside roughly 0% to +14%.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
